promptText: In the SQL Copilot pipeline, why is schema retrieval used instead of pasting the entire database schema into every prompt?
options: It keeps the prompt focused on relevant tables, reducing hallucination risk, token cost, and latency compared to dumping hundreds of irrelevant tables
LLMs have a hard technical limit of one table per API call
Pasting the full schema is actually safer, just slightly slower
Retrieval removes the need for the model to produce structured output
explanation: Dumping a large schema wastes tokens, buries relevant tables among irrelevant ones, and increases the chance of misread relationships; retrieval-based schema linking keeps the prompt small, cheap, and focused, mirroring the RAG principle of retrieving only relevant context.

promptText: Why must a SQL Copilot execute generated queries against a read-only database role or replica rather than a writable production connection?
options: A model can generate destructive or overly broad statements from misunderstanding or injection, and a read-only grant enforced at the database level makes irreversible damage impossible even if application-layer validation has a bug
Read replicas always return results faster than the primary database
Writable connections technically cannot execute SELECT statements
Read-only roles are a syntactic requirement of the SQL standard
explanation: Application-level checks can have bugs, but a database role with no write grants cannot be bypassed by a validation bug or a prompt injection, making read-only-by-default the single most important safety commitment in the design.

promptText: What does "schema grounding" mean in the context of a text-to-SQL system?
options: Giving the model an accurate, structured representation of the real database - tables, columns, keys, relationships - as context before generation, instead of letting it assume a 'typical' schema
Storing the schema exclusively inside a graph database
Training a brand-new model from scratch on your schema alone
Preventing the model from ever seeing any table name
explanation: Schema grounding is foundational because every downstream capability - correct joins, filters, aggregation grain - depends on the model reasoning about the real schema rather than a plausible but hallucinated one.

promptText: What does running EXPLAIN on a candidate query validate before execution?
options: That the query plan is executable, catching referential, type, and ambiguous-join errors without scanning or returning any actual rows - distinct from the later row-count cost gate
That the query automatically has a missing LIMIT clause added
How confident the model is in the query it generated
That sensitive columns are stripped from the result set before execution
explanation: EXPLAIN runs against the live database and catches referential errors, type errors, and ambiguous joins that a grammar-only SQL parser cannot see, and it does so as the cheapest possible pre-flight check before any cost/row-limit gate.

promptText: According to the chapter, what is the single most dangerous shortcut a team can take when building a SQL Copilot?
options: Executing the model's output directly against a writable production database connection "because the demo needs to feel real"
Logging every generated query and its explanation for later review
Using a real SQL parser to check syntax before execution
Retrieving only the top-K relevant tables instead of the full schema
explanation: This is explicitly called out as the single most dangerous shortcut - and exactly the one a demo deadline tempts engineers into taking - because a single bad generation against a writable connection can cause irreversible data loss.

promptText: Why are foreign key relationships explicitly included in the prompt even though they are already enforced by the database?
options: Database-level constraints don't automatically appear in a prompt just because they exist; the model must be told explicitly which columns join to which, since guessing from name similarity fails on surrogate keys or multiple plausible join paths
Foreign keys are removed from the schema catalog before indexing for performance reasons
SQL parsers cannot validate any query that references a foreign key
Few-shot examples are technically incapable of describing table relationships
explanation: Guessing a join key from name similarity alone fails on real-world schemas with surrogate keys or multiple plausible join paths; explicit FK metadata turns a guessing exercise into a reliable lookup.

promptText: A generated SQL query is syntactically flawless and every referenced column genuinely exists, yet it counts total orders instead of distinct customers when the user asked "how many customers ordered." Which layer of correctness has failed?
options: Intent correctness - the hardest layer to catch automatically, since it requires understanding what the user actually meant, not just what parses or resolves
Syntactic correctness
Referential correctness
Authorization correctness
explanation: A query can pass syntax and referential checks perfectly while still silently answering a slightly different question than intended - this invisible-unless-tested-for failure is the intent correctness layer.

promptText: Why is asking the model in a prompt to "only show data the user is authorized to see" not a valid access-control mechanism?
options: It is advisory rather than enforced - an unusual phrasing or prompt injection can bypass it, so authorization must be enforced by a deterministic policy layer independent of the model, ideally reinforced by database-level row-level security
Because natural-language instructions consume too many tokens to be practical at scale
Because access-control logic can only ever be expressed as SQL GRANT statements
Because the model cannot parse the word "authorized" without fine-tuning
explanation: The model cannot be the security boundary since it is a text generator with no reliable, tamper-proof concept of authorization; a deterministic policy engine plus database-level row-level security gives defense-in-depth so a single bug class can't cause a leak.

promptText: In schema retrieval, what is the risk of setting the top-K parameter too small?
options: A needed bridge/join table may be excluded from the prompt, causing the model to hallucinate a direct join that doesn't exist or produce wrong cardinality from a missing join condition
The vector store will run out of storage space
The model will always refuse to answer the question
Query execution will silently switch to a writable connection
explanation: K is a trade-off knob: too small risks missing a needed bridge table (a false negative producing a wrong join), while too large dilutes the prompt with irrelevant schema and increases cost and confusion.

promptText: What is semantic caching in a SQL Copilot, and why does it matter for cost?
options: Caching queries/results for recurring, semantically similar questions (e.g., "top customers this month" with only the date changing), which can eliminate the majority of model calls in a mature deployment
Encrypting the database's query planner statistics at rest
A compression algorithm applied directly to vector embeddings
A technique for caching the SQL parser's grammar rules
explanation: Organizational questions repeat constantly with only small variations like the date window; a well-tuned semantic cache turns a linear cost-per-question curve into something closer to flat.

promptText: A VP wants SQL Copilot to also handle simple writes like "mark this order as cancelled." What does the chapter recommend?
options: Constrain writes to a small, explicitly whitelisted set of parameterized, pre-reviewed tool-calling actions with mandatory human confirmation, rather than generating and executing arbitrary write SQL from natural language, since open-ended write generation is a fundamentally different, much higher-risk category
Allow the model to generate arbitrary UPDATE and DELETE statements as long as an EXPLAIN pass succeeds first
Grant the copilot a writable database role and rely on a Slack notification after each write executes
Refuse the request outright, since natural-language systems can never safely participate in any state-changing workflow
explanation: This converts an open-ended, hard-to-bound text-to-SQL-write problem into a bounded, auditable tool-calling problem with a fixed action surface, strict argument validation, human confirmation, and full audit logging.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend capping self-correction retries (feeding EXPLAIN errors back to the model) at roughly two to three attempts rather than allowing unlimited retries?
options: Beyond a few attempts, additional retries mostly add latency and cost without materially improving the success rate, and repeated failure can indicate the question is genuinely unanswerable against the available schema
Database engines physically reject a fourth EXPLAIN call within the same session
LLM providers contractually cap retries at three per API key
A fourth retry always produces a syntactically invalid query due to token truncation
explanation: After exhausting retries the system should fail gracefully - tell the user the question couldn't be translated, optionally show what was attempted, and offer to route to a human analyst rather than returning a possibly-wrong best guess.

promptText: Which statement best explains why the chapter describes a production SQL Copilot as "not an LLM that is good at SQL" but rather an orchestration system?
options: Grounding, validation, authorization, and safe execution are all responsibilities the LLM cannot be trusted to enforce on its own, so translation is wrapped by independent, deterministic components for each concern
Because SQL grammar is too complex for any current LLM architecture to learn reliably
Because industry regulations mandate a Java orchestration layer for any system touching financial data
Because the LLM in this design only ever produces natural-language explanations and never touches SQL directly
explanation: The problem statement bundles parsing, grounding, retrieval/access-control, and systems-security sub-problems that no single language-modeling capability can solve alone - hence an orchestration system wrapping the LLM's translation role.

promptText: When deciding between a large general-purpose foundation model and a smaller model fine-tuned/heavily few-shotted on your own schema for a SQL Copilot at scale, what does the chapter recommend?
options: Start with a large general-purpose model plus retrieval and few-shot examples for fast shipping with no training pipeline; once usage volume and verified (question, SQL) pairs accumulate, a smaller fine-tuned or distilled model often matches or exceeds accuracy at a fraction of the cost, but fine-tuning before sufficient real usage data exists is premature
Always default to the largest available model regardless of cost, since SQL accuracy is the only metric that matters at scale
Fine-tune a small model before any production traffic exists, since large general-purpose models cannot generate valid SQL
Avoid fine-tuning entirely in all cases, since a fine-tuned model can never outperform a general-purpose one
explanation: This frames the decision as a cost/latency/accuracy trade-off measured against a schema-specific evaluation set, favoring a large model early and a fine-tuned smaller model once enough verified production usage data exists.

promptText: Why does the chapter describe "referencing only real, authorized objects" as a retrieval and access-control problem rather than a pure language-modeling problem?
options: No amount of prompting alone guarantees a model never mentions an unseen column, and even when shown a full schema the model has no innate concept of row- or column-level permissions, so both must be enforced by separate mechanisms
Because access control only applies to NoSQL document stores, not relational databases
Because language models cannot process column names longer than ten characters
Because retrieval systems automatically enforce authorization as a side effect of embedding similarity
explanation: Ensuring queries reference only real, authorized objects requires a retrieval mechanism to ground real identifiers and a deterministic access-control layer to enforce permissions - neither of which the LLM can guarantee unaided.
